name: Diagnostic_LGE-LLG_1
questiontext:
Given that \(p={{CT:0}}\) and \(q={{CT:1}}\) give \({{CT:2}}\) as a function of \(p\) and \(q\).

[[input:ans1]]

[[validation:ans1]]
generalfeedback: Below are the basic rules of logarithms. alg_logarithms Given \(p={{CT:0}}\) and \(q={{CT:1}}\) then, \[{{CT:2}} = \ln \left({{CT:3}}\right)+{{CT:1}} = {{CT:4}} = {{CT:5}}.\]

on_true.feedback: You seem to have that \(\ln\left(x^{{CT:6}}\right)=\left(\ln \left( x \right) \right)^{{CT:6}}\). This is only true given \(x=1\), in which case \[\ln \left(x\right) = \ln \left({{CT:3}}\right) = \left(\ln \left( x \right) \right)^{{CT:6}} = \ln \left(1\right) = 0.\] In general \[\ln \left({{CT:3}}\right) = {{CT:7}}.\]
You seem to have that \(\ln\left(xmy\right)\) is \(\ln \left( xm \right)\) multiplied by \(\ln \left( x \right)\). In general \[\ln\left(xmy\right)=\ln \left( xm \right)+\ln \left( x \right).\]
